ui.qs: Tap the mic and say the word
ui.nm: No microphone here. Practice with pairs or dictation instead.

vow.x: Japanese has five short vowels: a, i, u, e, o. Each is clear and steady, never gliding. U is said with flat, relaxed lips, not rounded like English “oo”: うえ, あお.

long.x: A long vowel lasts two beats and can change the meaning: おばさん (aunt) vs おばあさん (grandmother). Hold the vowel for one full extra beat; ー in katakana and おう, えい in hiragana are long.

sokuon.x: Small っ is a silent one-beat pause before the next consonant: きて (come) vs きって (stamp). Shape your mouth for the next sound, wait one beat, then release.

nn.x: ん counts as its own beat. It sounds like m before p, b, m (さんぽ), n before t, d, n (せんせい) and ng before k, g (にほんご). Do not swallow it: こな vs こんな.

yoon.x: Small ゃ ゅ ょ join the kana before them into ONE beat: きょう (today, 2 beats) vs きよう (skillful, 3 beats); びょういん (hospital) vs びよういん (hair salon).

pitch.x: Tokyo Japanese uses high and low pitch, not stress. Words that look the same can differ only in pitch: はꜜし (chopsticks, high–low) vs はしꜜ (bridge, low–high, then a drop). ꜜ marks where the pitch falls.

devoice.x: Between voiceless consonants or at the end of a word, i and u are often whispered: です sounds close to “des”, すき to “ski”, ひと to “hto”. Keep the beat, just drop the voice.

tsu.x: つ is “ts” as in “cats”; す is a plain s. Touch the ridge behind your upper teeth, then release: つき (moon) vs すき (like).
